attributes.title: Level 9

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you list out the project’s scenes in a multi-line comment, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of pet might you use for this project?

❓ What types of activities might the pet complete in a typical day? 

❓ Where might each scene take place in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has typed /* */ with several spaces in between to create a multiline comment in the editor.

💡 Prompt the ninja to first identify a pet that they’d like to use in their project. If they have a pet at home, it’s a good idea to use that as inspiration. If not, encourage the ninja to brainstorm other animals (or an imaginary pet!) that they are knowledgeable about.

💡 Once the ninja has selected a pet to use for their project, help them brainstorm different activities that the pet might complete in a day. In this project, the ninja will be creating each scene in pixel art, so it’s useful to think of simple scenes. Prompt the ninja to arrange the scenes in a logical order that might match the order that the pet might complete them in.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by brainstorming the different scenes in the project!


At the top of the editor, type /* */ to create a multi-line comment. Place the cursor between the asterisks, then press Enter multiple times to create multiple lines within the comment.


This project will allow the user to experience the day in the life of a pet. Inside the comment, list out scenes 0-7. Scene 0 will be the title screen, scene 1 will introduce the pet, and scene 7 will be the ending screen. 


Brainstorm what kind of animal the pet will be, then list out activities the pet might complete in its day in scenes 2-6. The activities should take place in 2 different settings (for example, going for a walk outside or eating breakfast indoors).

steps.hints: ❓ Did you draw solid layers in each scene’s image to show the foreground and background, then use pixel art techniques to add detail to each image, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What colors might you use for the title and end screens?

❓ What backgrounds might you add to each image to show where each activity is taking place?

❓ What images might be drawn to each scene to show what activity is taking place?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja brainstorm how to depict the activity in each scene and its setting. Remind the ninja that each background image should include a mix of detailed and solid areas. Encourage the ninja to use a variety of pixel art techniques that they’ve learned about to draw the pet and other images that illustrate what’s happening in each scene. As needed, prompt the ninja to look at existing background images in the gallery for ideas in customizing the background of each scene.

💡 Point out the different tools in the paint editor that can be helpful for designing a 160x120 image. The zoom in/zoom out tools on the bottom right corner can be helpful for focusing on one area of the image at a time. The marquee tool is useful for rearranging a specific part of the image. The canvas pan tool can also be used to drag the image around the editor to see the different parts of the image more closely. The ninja can also select different brush sizes to draw at different scales.
steps.instructions:
Design background images for each scene of the project!


Create 160x120 image assets in the Assets menu for the title and end screens. Fill each asset with a solid color so that text and other imagery can be added later. Give each asset a descriptive name.


Create 6 more 160x120 image assets to use for scenes 1-6 in the project. Give each asset a descriptive name that tells its scene number, like this: scene1Screen.


Each image should display the setting that the activity is taking place in and any other images that show what’s happening in the scene.


Start by using solid colors to create clear layers in each background image, defining the foreground and background of the scene. Add details in the image to show where actions are taking place, then use pixel art techniques (such as dithering, complementary colors, and highlights/shadows) to add depth to each part of the image. Consider which aspects require the most detail and which can be left mostly solid. Use tools in the paint editor (such as zoom in/out, marquee, and canvas pan) to focus attention on one part of the image at a time.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an if conditional to check if the value of sceneNum is equal to 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the callScene function is called, and 0 is passed as the argument?

❓ How do you define a function with a number parameter?

❓ What else might be added to the title screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the callScene function is called with 0 passed as the argument, the title screen image asset will be displayed on screen.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation if they need help adding a number parameter to the function or adding the conditional code inside of the function.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what else might be added to the title screen to engage the user. Later in the project, a text image layer will be added with text sprite directions.
steps.instructions:
Display the title scene image on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // project initialization comment below the comment that lists all of the scenes. 


Underneath, define a callScene function with a sceneNum number parameter. If sceneNum is equal to 0, set the background image to the title scene image asset. 


Then, add a // project start comment and call the function, passing 0 as the argument to test the background image. 


Click ▶ to see the title scene background image appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you test to see if the correct scene image is displayed on screen when the matching scene number is passed to the callScene function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image asset should be used as the image parameter in each setBackgroundImage function?

❓ How can each setBackgroundImage function be tested?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to check that the scene number in each image asset of the setBackgroundImage functions matches the number that is checked for in each corresponding condition.

💡 To test that the correct number screen appears in each condition, the ninja can type different numbers inside the parentheses of the callScene function call.
steps.instructions:
Display the matching background image when each scene is called!


Repeat the previous step with the remaining scenes. Inside the callScene function definition, add 7 else if conditions that check if sceneNum is equal to each scene’s number. 


Inside each else if condition, set the background image to the corresponding image asset that matches each scene number.


Pass different numbers to the callScene function call to test out each scene.


Click ▶ to see each scene’s image appear when different numbers are passed to the callScene function.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the foreground (color of the text) and background (color behind the text) parameters to create a strong contrast between the text and the background image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the printDialog function do? How might it be used in a project?

❓ What text might be printed on the screen in scene 1 of the project?

❓ What colors should the foreground and background parameters be set to to create a strong contrast between the text and the background image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the Story extension, there are several different functions that print text to the screen, but they vary in style, position, and uses. The printDialog function prints text to the screen within a given box, relative to the camera, character by character. This can be useful for telling a story, showing sprites having a conversation, or giving a message to the user.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use scene 1 of the project to introduce their pet. This might include the pet’s name, what type of animal it is, and how they start their day. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to test the printDialog function by passing 1 to the callScene function. The ninja should tinker with each of the parameters to make sure the text is clearly legible on screen.
steps.instructions:
Use the Story extension to add dialog text to the project! 


Click Extensions, then scroll down to select the arcade-story extension to add it to the project.


Open Story, then drag [print (:)) at camera x (80) y (90) in box width (150) height (50)] inside the else if condition in the callScene function definition that checks if sceneNum is equal to 1. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

story.printDialog(":)", 80, 90, 50, 150)

The printDialog function prints text to the screen within a given box, relative to the camera, character by character. It takes 8 possible parameters: text, x-position, y-position, height of box, width of box, foreground color, background color, and text speed.


Update the text parameter to introduce the pet and ask the user what the pet should do next. Tinker with the values of the remaining parameters to place the text on screen and create a visible contrast with the background image, so that the text is clearly legible.


Update the callScene function call to test the dialog text in scene 1. 


Click ▶ to see text that introduces the pet! Update the parameters to make sure the text is positioned correctly on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you tell what the pet is doing in each printDialog function, then ask the user what the pet should do next in each scene except for 6?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What text might be printed on the screen in each of the remaining scenes?

❓ What might happen in scene 6 of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In each printDialog function, the ninja should describe what the pet is doing in each scene. The ninja should test the project repeatedly to make sure the background image and dialog text matches in each scene. The ninja should tinker with the parameters in each printDialog function to position the text and set the foreground and background parameters to make the dialog text clearly legible on screen.

💡 The ninja does not need to ask the user what the pet should do next in scene 6 because the scene will transition to the end screen, culminating the project.
steps.instructions:
Add text that tells what’s happening in each scene of the project!


Repeat the previous step with the remaining scenes. Open Scene and drag [print (:)) at camera x (80) y (90) in box width (150) height (50)] inside the else if conditions in the callScene function definition that check if sceneNum is equal to 2-6. 


In each scene, update the text parameter to tell what the pet is doing and then ask the user what the pet should do next. In scene 6, do not ask the user what the pet should do next. 


Update the callScene function call to test the dialog text in each scene. 


Click ▶ to see text that introduces the pet! Update the parameters to make sure the text is positioned correctly and stands out on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you consider what choices the user might be given after they select a scene?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What choices might be stored in each question array?

❓ What choices might the user be given in each scene? Which scene should they go to next?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to think through the chronological order of each of the scenes. It might be useful for the ninja to identify the first two choices that include two very different scenes (e.g. different locations). From there, they can identify similar scenes that might flow logically. 

💡 As needed, work together with a ninja to build out a logic map, as shown below, to identify the flow between scenes before adding code in the next step.

💡 Remind the ninja to store multiple options in each array and to double check that the user won’t end up on the scene that they are currently on. It’s also okay for a user to circle back to the same screen in order to reduce the additional number of specific options needed in the project.
steps.instructions:
Create questions to determine the user’s path in the project!


Under // project initialization but above the callScene function definition, create 5 arrays. Use the question number in each array’s name, like this: questionOne. 


Inside each array, store 2 strings that will lead the user to a specific scene, based on their answer. Using the multi-line scene comment at the top of the guide, match each question array’s number to the scene number that it will be used in.


Think through the sequence of each step and which activity might make sense for the pet to complete first or choose between. When adding elements to each array, consider what will happen when the user makes their first choice, then their second, and so on. As needed, build out a logic map to identify the different paths that the user might take during the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check if the user’s last answer is equal to questionOne[0] or questionOne[1] in the if/else if conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do the showPlayerchoices and checkLastAnswer functions do? How might they be used in a project?

❓ What possible scenes might the user be taken to in scene 1 of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The showPlayerchoices function presents a menu of options on the screen, from which the user can select. The checkLastAnswer function accesses the user’s selection from the showPlayerchoices menu. The functions can be used together to personalize a project, based on the user’s response.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use their multi-line scene comment, their logic map (if created), and the questionOne array to identify which scene number should be passed to the callScene function in scene 1, depending on the user’s response.
steps.instructions:
Provide the user with choices to determine what scene they’ll go to next!


Open Story and drag [show player choices (choice1) (choice2)] inside the else if condition in the callScene function definition that checks if sceneNum is equal to 1.


Set the choice parameters to the elements at the 0 and 1 index of the questionOne array, like this: story.showPlayerChoices

﻿(questionOne[0], questionOne[1])


Create an if/else if conditional below, then open Story again and drag [last answer equals (choice)] into the parentheses of each condition. Update the choice parameters in the if and else if conditions to check for the two possible choices from the questionOne array. Inside each condition, call the callScene function, passing the scene number that matches the answer selected as the argument.


Update the callScene function call under // project start to test the choice in scene 1.


Click ▶ to make different scenes appear on screen, based on the user’s response!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you test out the checkLastAnswer code in each condition to make sure that the next scene matches the user’s response?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What scene numbers should be passed to the callScene function in each scene?

❓ What should happen in scene 6 of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to repeatedly test the project by passing 1 to the the callScene function and selecting different paths along the way. If they notice they are taken to a scene that doesn’t match their choice, prompt the ninja to update their code to make sure logic is correct.
steps.instructions:
Create a personalized experience for the user by changing scenes based on their response!


Repeat the previous step with scenes 2-5. Open Story and drag [last answer equals (choice)] into the parentheses of the conditions that check if sceneNum is equal to 2-5. 


Add an if/else if conditional inside each condition that checks the value of the user’s last answer. Call the callScene function inside each condition, passing the scene number that matches the answer selected as the argument.


If sceneNum is equal to 6, call the callScene function to display scene 7 to end the project.


Update the callScene function call under // project start to test the choices in each scene. Pass 1 as the argument to begin at the first scene. Test out different responses to make sure all of the possible options work as intended and update the logic code as needed.


Click ▶ to experience the pet’s day differently, based on the user’s response!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you press Alt + Shift and a color number key to outline the title text, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might a new image asset be created to draw the title of the project on?

❓ How is drawing the title in an image asset similar and different to creating a text sprite for the project title?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 There are many different ways to add a title to a project. The ninja can draw the title in an image with a background filled in behind it, they can use a separate image asset to draw the text, they can use a text sprite or the story extension, or have a sprite say the title. Creating a separate image asset for the title text allows the ninja to edit both the text and the background image more easily, without interfering with one another.

💡 If the ninja wants to add other images from the gallery onto the title text image, they can create a new image asset, then copy the pixel art and paste it onto the title text image.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the hexadecimal counting system is used here to select from the 15 colors in the color palette. The hexadecimal system is a base-16 counting system that uses A-F for the decimal (base-10) numbers 10-15. The ninja can use Alt + Shift + a number 1-9 to select from colors 1-9, and Alt + Shift + a letter key A-F to select from colors 10-15.
steps.instructions:
Design text to add to the title screen!


Create a 160x120 image asset in the Assets menu. A different image asset will be used to place the title text on top of the background image. This will make the title easier to edit, without affecting the background image.


Think of a descriptive title for the project, then use the paint tool to draw text displaying the name. Position the text towards the top of the canvas, and create large enough letters so that the title will be easily visible on screen. To create contrast, press Alt + Shift and a color number key to outline the text on the canvas. Use letters A-F to access colors 10 through 15.


Add any other images to personalize the title screen! Name the image asset titleTextImage. 


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create a sprite with its image set to the title image asset if sceneNum is equal to 0. Pass 0 to the callScene function call under // project start to see the title appear.


Click ▶ to see the title of the project displayed on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the parameters in the textsprite.create function to share directions with the user?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the Text Sprite extension be used for? 

❓ What do the foreground and background color parameters in the textsprite.create function represent?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the Text Sprite extension is useful for creating a string of text that remains on the screen. The extension has many text customization functions, such as setting its outline, the font size/style, its border, and its image icon.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the foreground parameter of the textsprite.create function represents the color of the text and the background parameter represents the color that appears behind the text. Have the ninja consider what colors to use for each parameter, to make the text clearly stand out on screen.
steps.instructions:
Add directions to the title screen!


Click Extensions, then scroll down to select the arcade-text extension to add it to the project.


Open Text Sprite and drag [text sprite (text)] underneath the title sprite code in the scene 0 conditional. 


Give the text sprite a descriptive name. Then, update the text to tell the user to press any button to begin and tinker with the background (color behind the text) and foreground (color of the text) parameters to make the text stand out clearly against the title screen background.


Click ▶ to see the directions appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you tinker with the position of the text sprite to make the directions appear clearly on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What number might you set the text sprite’s font height to? 

❓ How do the font styles change as the font’s height is updated?



Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the Text Sprite extension creates text sizes that are multiples of 5 or 8. Any other number used as the argument in the setMaxFontHeight function will not change the size of the text. If the ninja is unfamiliar with the concept of multiples, provide a few examples for 5 (5, 10, 15, 20) and 8 (8, 16, 24, 32) that they can tinker with in their code.

💡 If the font size is a multiple of 5, it will have a different font style than if it is a multiple of 8.
steps.instructions:
Update the size and positioning of the text sprite so that it is clearly visible.


Open Text Sprite and drag [set (textSprite) max font height (height)] underneath the code that creates the text sprite. 


Below, position the text sprite so that it appears below the title text, in the center of the screen. 


Click ▶ to test the size and positioning of the direction text!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you pause the project until the user presses a button, before scene 1 is called?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function do? Why might it be useful in a project?

❓ What function should be used to destroy the title and direction sprites on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function pauses the project until a user presses a button. This is useful for creating a title screen that the user can view, then when they’re ready, they can press a button to begin the game.

💡The pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function is a secret menu function that can only be accessed by typing controller and a dot operator, then selecting the function from the code completion tool.
steps.instructions:
Reset the scene before the next scene is called!


Underneath the code that sets the text sprite’s position, type controller and a dot operator, then select pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses () to call the function. 


Underneath, add code to destroy the title and direction sprites. Then, call the callScene function to display scene 1 on screen. 


Click ▶ to test the title and direction code. Notice how a button needs to be pressed in order for the project to display the next scene!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the pet sprite’s z-property, so that it appears in front of the scene’s background image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What pixel art techniques might you use to create a unique pet image asset?

❓ Where should the pet sprite be placed on screen? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja open their scene 1 background image asset before designing the pet image asset. Prompt the ninja to identify where the pet image might be placed in the scene and what canvas dimensions might work best for the pet image. Then, have the ninja create their pet image asset using several different pixel art techniques (such as dithering, highlights/shadows, complementary colors, etc.).

💡 Make sure the ninja has added code to destroy the pet sprite before the conditional in scene 1.
steps.instructions:
Personalize the first scene that introduces the pet!


Create a new image asset in the Assets menu. Design a pet sprite image that can be used in front of the scene 1 background image. Resize the canvas, so that the pet image appears larger against the background image. Use pixel art techniques to add depth to the pet sprite’s design. Give the image asset a descriptive name.


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create a sprite with its image set to the pet image asset in scene 1, above the printDialog function. 


Position the sprite so that it appears in an appropriate spot against the background image. Set the sprite’s z-property so that it appears in front of the background image and text on screen.


Destroy the pet sprite after the choice menu appears, before the next scene is called.


Click ▶ to test the pet sprite’s appearance in the scene where it’s introduced!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a dot operator and the playUntilDone function to pause the project, before it resets?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What message might be shared with the user in the printDialog function?

❓ How is drawing the end title in an image asset similar and different to creating a text sprite for the end screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 There are many different ways to add a title to a project. The ninja can draw the title in an image with a background filled in behind it, they can use a separate image asset to draw the text, they can use a text sprite or the story extension, or have a sprite say the title. Creating a separate image asset for the title text allows the ninja to edit both the text and the background image more easily, without interfering with one another.

💡 If the ninja wants to add other images from the gallery onto the end title text image, they can create a new image asset, then copy the pixel art and paste it onto the end title text image.

💡 Point out to the ninja that Alt + Shift + a color number key is a useful tool for easily outlining the text in a different color to make it stand out on screen. The ninja should use Alt + Shift + A-F to access colors 10-15 in the color palette
steps.instructions:
Create an ending scene for the project!


Open the Assets menu and duplicate the title image asset. Update the asset name, then edit the text drawn on the image to signal the end of the project. Press Alt + Shift and a color number (0-9) or letter key (A-F) to outline the text on the canvas.


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create a sprite in scene 7 with its image set to the ending text image asset. 


Open Story and drag [print (:)) at camera x (80) y (90) in box width (150) height (50)] underneath. Update the parameters so that the text appears correctly and shares an ending message with the user.


Below, add code to play a melody until it finishes, then reset the game.


Click ▶ to experience the completed project in different ways!

subgroups.title: A Pet’s Day
subgroups.introduction: Create a “choose your own adventure” project that uses the Story and Text Sprite extensions to create a personalized experience for the user.

validationItems.text: Use a multi-line comment to plan out each scene in the project’s story sequence.
Use a callScene function with a sceneNum number parameter to call the different background image assets.
Add dialog text to tell what’s happening in each scene.
Create 5 question arrays with 2 elements in each.
Provide the user with 2 choices, then call a specific scene based on the user response.
Design a background image layer with text and an image that appears on top of the background for both the splash and ending screens.
Use a text sprite to provide directions on the title screen.
Call the first scene after any button is pressed.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 9 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about adding User Interface (UI) features, such as splash and game over screens, user choice, and game narrative that can significantly improve the User Experience (UX) of a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 9:

badges.title: Screen Time
badges.description: Use a variety of pixel art techniques to create full-screen image assets to enhance the user experience in a project.

badges.title: An Asset for Every Season
badges.description: Create 160x120 full-screen image assets that can be layered on top of one another to create a variety of game screens.

badges.title: Flavor Text
badges.description: Use the Text Sprite extension to create custom scene titles, directions, and variable counters on screen.

badges.title: Choose Your Adventure
badges.description: Create a personalized experience for the user by changing scenes based on their responses.

badges.title: Reliable Narrator
badges.description: Use the Story extension to create narrative scenes that describe what’s happening in the project.

badges.title: Chain of Command
badges.description: Convert a number value to a string.

badges.title: Red Light Green Light
badges.description: Pause a project until any button is pressed to make screens remain as long as a user chooses.
